lessons.title: What Is an Array?
lessons.content: An array stores elements in contiguous memory slots, numbered from 0. Because the slots sit right next to each other, the computer can jump straight to any index by computing base_address + index * element_size — no searching involved. That's what makes reading nums[7] just as fast as reading nums[0], no matter how big the array is. The trade-off: inserting or removing an element in the middle means shifting every element after it, which costs O(n).

conceptChecks.question: Why is accessing an element by index O(1) in an array?
options: Because the array is sorted
Because its memory address can be computed directly from the index
Because arrays cache the last accessed element
Because arrays use a hash function on the index
conceptChecks.explanation: Elements sit at contiguous addresses, so index i's address is just base_address + i * element_size — a calculation, not a search.

conceptChecks.question: What is the time complexity of inserting an element at the beginning of an array of size n?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
conceptChecks.explanation: Every existing element has to shift one slot to the right to make room, which touches all n elements.

lessons.title: Strings as Character Arrays
lessons.content: A string is essentially an array of characters, which is why so many array techniques — two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums — apply directly to string problems. One key gotcha: in many languages (Java, Python, Kotlin) strings are immutable. Every 'modification' actually builds a brand-new string, so concatenating in a tight loop is quietly O(n^2) unless you use a mutable builder.

conceptChecks.question: Why do string problems often reuse array techniques like two pointers?
options: Strings are always stored on the heap
A string is fundamentally an array of characters
Strings are always sorted
Strings can't be indexed
conceptChecks.explanation: Indexable, contiguous character storage is exactly what makes array techniques transfer over.

conceptChecks.question: In many languages, why is repeatedly concatenating strings in a loop inefficient?
options: Because strings are immutable and each concatenation creates a new string
Because strings are stored in a linked list
Because concatenation requires sorting
Because strings can only be modified in place
conceptChecks.explanation: Each '+' allocates a new string and copies both old strings into it, so n concatenations cost O(n^2) total.

lessons.title: The Two-Pointer Technique
lessons.content: Instead of nested loops checking every pair (O(n^2)), two pointers walk through the array with two indices — either moving toward each other from both ends, or moving in the same direction at different speeds — cutting the work to O(n). This works when there's a monotonic property to exploit, most commonly on a sorted array: if the current pair's sum is too big, moving the right pointer left only makes it smaller; too small, moving the left pointer right only makes it bigger.

conceptChecks.question: What lets two pointers replace a nested loop and drop from O(n^2) to O(n)?
options: The array is stored as a linked list
A monotonic property lets you rule out a whole range of pairs after one comparison
Two pointers always sort the array first
Two pointers only work on strings
conceptChecks.explanation: Each comparison eliminates a range of remaining pairs, so the total work is linear instead of quadratic.

conceptChecks.question: In the classic 'pair sum equals target' problem on a sorted array, what do you do when the current pair's sum is too small?
options: Move the left pointer right, to increase the sum
Move the right pointer right
Restart from the beginning
Swap the two pointers
conceptChecks.explanation: Moving left rightward brings in a bigger value, increasing the sum toward the target.

lessons.title: Sliding Window
lessons.content: Sliding window is two pointers with a twist: instead of both ends of the array, they mark the boundaries of a 'window' that expands and shrinks as it slides across the data. Expand the right edge to include more elements; shrink the left edge when the window breaks some condition (too big a sum, a repeated character, etc.). This avoids recomputing from scratch for every window position — you just add what enters and remove what leaves.

conceptChecks.question: What's the key efficiency idea behind sliding window?
options: Recompute the entire window's answer from scratch every time it moves
Only add what newly enters the window and remove what leaves it, instead of recomputing
Sort the array before sliding
Use recursion to check every possible window
conceptChecks.explanation: Incremental add/remove is what keeps sliding window at O(n) instead of O(n * window size).

conceptChecks.question: When would you shrink the window from the left?
options: Every single step, regardless of the window's contents
When the window currently violates the condition you're maintaining (e.g. sum too large, a duplicate found)
Only after reaching the end of the array
Never — sliding window only expands
conceptChecks.explanation: Shrinking is how the window gets back to a valid state once expanding the right edge broke the condition.

lessons.title: Why HashMaps Are Fast
lessons.content: A HashMap stores key-value pairs by running each key through a hash function that converts it into an array index, then storing the value there. That's what gives average O(1) insert, lookup, and delete — no scanning required. Two different keys can hash to the same index (a collision); a good implementation handles this by storing the colliding keys together at that slot (e.g. in a small list) and comparing keys directly when needed. Worst case, with a bad hash function or too many collisions, this degrades to O(n).

conceptChecks.question: What gives a well-implemented HashMap its average O(1) lookup time?
options: It keeps keys sorted
A hash function maps keys almost directly to a storage index
It uses binary search internally
It stores all keys in a linked list
conceptChecks.explanation: The hash function computes a storage location directly from the key, skipping the need to search.

conceptChecks.question: What happens when two different keys hash to the same index (a collision)?
options: The second key silently overwrites the first
The HashMap immediately resizes to twice its size
The colliding keys are stored together at that index and compared individually when needed
The insert operation fails
conceptChecks.explanation: Collision handling (chaining or similar) keeps both keys retrievable instead of losing one.

lessons.title: When HashMaps Are the Right Tool
lessons.content: Watch for phrases like 'have I seen this before', 'count occurrences of', or 'need O(1) lookup' — these almost always point to a HashMap or HashSet. They're the wrong tool when order matters (a plain HashMap gives no ordering guarantee — use a LinkedHashMap or TreeMap if you need one) or when you need range queries (e.g. 'all keys between X and Y'), which need a sorted structure instead.

conceptChecks.question: You need to check if a value has appeared before while scanning a list once — what's the go-to structure?
options: A sorted array with binary search on every check
A HashSet, since membership checks are O(1) on average
A doubly linked list
A binary tree
conceptChecks.explanation: HashSet membership checks are O(1) on average, which is exactly what a single-pass 'seen before' check needs.

conceptChecks.question: Why is a plain HashMap usually a poor fit when you need results returned in sorted order?
options: HashMaps can't store more than 100 elements
HashMaps don't preserve or guarantee any particular key ordering
HashMaps are slower than arrays for every single operation
HashMaps can only store strings
conceptChecks.explanation: A plain HashMap gives no ordering guarantee, so you'd need a sort afterward or a different structure entirely.

lessons.title: What Are Data Structures & Algorithms?
lessons.content: A data structure is a way of organizing and storing data so it can be accessed and modified efficiently — a list, a stack, a tree. An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure or formula for solving a problem — sorting a list, finding a path. They're two sides of the same coin: the data structure you pick determines which algorithms are fast. A sorted array makes binary search possible; an unsorted one doesn't.
lessons.codeExample:
# A data structure (Python list) holding data,
# and an algorithm (built-in sort) operating on it
scores = [88, 42, 95, 67, 71]

sorted_scores = sorted(scores)          # algorithm: Timsort, O(n log n)
print(sorted_scores)                    # [42, 67, 71, 88, 95]
print(scores[2])                        # data structure: O(1) index access -> 95

lessons.title: Time and Space Complexity (Big-O)
lessons.content: Time complexity measures how an algorithm's running time grows as a function of input size. Space complexity measures how much extra working memory it needs. Both are expressed with Big-O notation, which describes the growth rate, not an exact time: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n) linearithmic, O(n^2) quadratic. Knowing these lets you predict how code will behave on larger inputs before you run it — the basis for performance optimization, resource management, and system design decisions.

lessons.title: Arrays in Practice
lessons.content: Use cases: storing a collection of elements, implementing other structures like stacks and queues, and building dynamic programming tables. Python's list is a dynamic array — it resizes automatically, but appending near the front or middle still shifts elements.
lessons.codeExample:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(nums[2])          # O(1) access -> 30
nums.append(50)         # add to the end, O(1) amortized
nums.insert(0, 5)       # insert at front -> shifts every element, O(n)
print(nums)             # [5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

lessons.title: Linked Lists in Practice
lessons.content: A linked list is a chain of nodes, each pointing to the next. Use cases: dynamic memory allocation (no need to know the size upfront), implementing stacks/queues, and undo functionality — each undo step is just 'move to the previous node'.

lessons.title: Stacks in Practice
lessons.content: A stack is Last-In-First-Out (LIFO). Use cases: expression evaluation and syntax parsing (matching brackets), backtracking algorithms, and managing function calls in recursion — every recursive call pushes a new frame onto the call stack.
lessons.codeExample:
stack = []
stack.append(1)   # push
stack.append(2)
stack.append(3)
print(stack.pop())  # 3 - Last In, First Out
print(stack)         # [1, 2]

lessons.title: Queues in Practice
lessons.content: A queue is First-In-First-Out (FIFO). Use cases: task scheduling, breadth-first search, and managing requests in the order they arrive — the first task queued is the first one processed.
lessons.codeExample:
from collections import deque

queue = deque()
queue.append("task1")   # enqueue
queue.append("task2")
queue.append("task3")
print(queue.popleft())  # "task1" - First In, First Out
print(queue)             # deque(['task2', 'task3'])

lessons.title: Trees in Practice
lessons.content: A tree is a hierarchical structure of parent-child nodes. Use cases: representing file systems, binary search trees for efficient searching and sorting, and decision-making algorithms (each node is a decision point).
lessons.codeExample:
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.left = None
        self.right = None

root = TreeNode(10)
root.left = TreeNode(5)
root.right = TreeNode(15)

def inorder(node):
    if node:
        inorder(node.left)
        print(node.value, end=" ")
        inorder(node.right)

inorder(root)   # 5 10 15 (sorted order for a BST)

lessons.title: Graphs in Practice
lessons.content: A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges, which can be directed or weighted. Use cases: social network analysis, shortest-path routing in maps, and dependency resolution (e.g. package managers deciding install order).

lessons.title: Hash Tables in Practice
lessons.content: A hash table maps keys to values using a hash function, giving average O(1) lookup. Use cases: implementing associative arrays, database indexing, and caching — storing an expensive result keyed by its input so it's never recomputed.

lessons.title: Bubble Sort
lessons.content: Repeatedly steps through the list, swapping adjacent elements that are out of order, until nothing needs swapping. Simple to understand and implement, but O(n^2) — inefficient for large datasets. Mostly useful for teaching, or tiny inputs.

lessons.title: Merge Sort
lessons.content: A divide-and-conquer algorithm: split the array in half recursively until each piece has one element, then merge the pieces back together in sorted order. O(n log n) and stable (equal elements keep their relative order), which makes it a solid default for large datasets.

lessons.title: Quick Sort
lessons.content: Also divide-and-conquer: pick a pivot, partition the array into elements smaller and larger than it, then recursively sort each side. Average O(n log n) and generally faster in practice than Merge Sort due to better cache behavior, though not stable and worst-case O(n^2) on a bad pivot choice.

lessons.title: Insertion Sort
lessons.content: Builds the final sorted array one element at a time, inserting each new element into its correct position among the already-sorted elements. O(n^2) worst case, but very efficient for small or nearly-sorted datasets — often used as the base case inside faster hybrid sorts.

lessons.title: Linear Search
lessons.content: Checks every element in order until it finds a match, or reaches the end. O(n), but it's the only option on unsorted data — there's no shortcut without some structure to exploit.

lessons.title: Binary Search
lessons.content: On a sorted array, repeatedly checks the middle element and discards the half that can't contain the target. O(log n) — doubling the input size only adds one more comparison. This is the payoff for keeping data sorted.

lessons.title: Depth-First Search (DFS)
lessons.content: Explores as far as possible down one branch before backtracking, using recursion or an explicit stack. Use cases: exploring all reachable nodes, detecting cycles, and topological sorting.

lessons.title: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
lessons.content: Explores level by level, visiting all of a node's neighbors before moving further out, using a queue. Use case: finding the shortest path in an unweighted graph — the first time you reach a node is guaranteed to be via the shortest route.

lessons.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
lessons.content: Finds the shortest path from a start node to every other node in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights, using a priority queue to always expand the closest unvisited node next. Use case: network routing, where edge weights represent latency or distance.

lessons.title: Memoization
lessons.content: A top-down DP technique: cache the result of each expensive function call so repeated calls with the same input return instantly instead of recomputing. Turns naive recursive solutions with exponential blow-up (like plain recursive Fibonacci) into fast ones.

lessons.title: Tabulation
lessons.content: A bottom-up DP technique: build a table of subproblem results iteratively, starting from the smallest subproblems, so each larger answer is assembled from already-known smaller ones. Avoids recursion overhead entirely.

lessons.title: Greedy Algorithms
lessons.content: A greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping it leads to a globally optimal solution — and for certain problems (Huffman coding for data compression, activity selection, Kruskal's and Prim's algorithms for minimum spanning trees) it provably does. The classic example below: pick activities by earliest finish time to fit as many non-overlapping activities as possible.
lessons.codeExample:
def activity_selection(activities):
    # activities: list of (start, end), will be sorted by end time
    activities = sorted(activities, key=lambda a: a[1])
    selected = [activities[0]]
    last_end = activities[0][1]
    for start, end in activities[1:]:
        if start >= last_end:
            selected.append((start, end))
            last_end = end
    return selected

activities = [(1, 3), (2, 4), (3, 5), (0, 6), (5, 7)]
print(activity_selection(activities))   # [(1, 3), (3, 5), (5, 7)]

lessons.title: Arrays: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's Algorithm)
lessons.content: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum. Kadane's insight: at each position, either extend the previous subarray or start fresh from here — whichever gives a bigger sum. O(n), single pass. Use cases: financial data analysis (best trading window), game development (best streak).
lessons.codeExample:
def max_subarray(nums):
    best = current = nums[0]
    for num in nums[1:]:
        current = max(num, current + num)
        best = max(best, current)
    return best

print(max_subarray([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]))   # 6  ([4, -1, 2, 1])

lessons.title: Arrays: Two Sum
lessons.content: Find two numbers in an array that add up to a target. The naive approach checks every pair, O(n^2); a hash map remembers what you've seen so each element only needs one O(1) lookup for its complement, giving O(n) overall.

lessons.title: Linked Lists: Detect a Cycle
lessons.content: Floyd's cycle detection ('tortoise and hare'): move one pointer one step at a time and another two steps at a time. If there's a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually lap the slow one and they'll meet; if there's no cycle, the fast pointer reaches the end first. O(n) time, O(1) space.

lessons.title: Linked Lists: Reverse a Linked List
lessons.content: Walk the list once, and at each node flip its `next` pointer to point backward instead of forward, tracking the previous node as you go. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
lessons.codeExample:
def reverse_linked_list(head):
    prev = None
    current = head
    while current:
        next_node = current.next
        current.next = prev
        prev = current
        current = next_node
    return prev

lessons.title: Stacks & Queues: Implement a Queue Using Two Stacks
lessons.content: A classic problem that shows how the two structures relate: push new items onto an 'in' stack; when you need to dequeue, pour everything into an 'out' stack (reversing the order) if it's empty, then pop from that. Each element moves between stacks at most once, so operations are O(1) amortized.

lessons.title: Trees: Traversals and Lowest Common Ancestor
lessons.content: Inorder (left, node, right), preorder (node, left, right), and postorder (left, right, node) traversals visit every node in a different order — inorder gives sorted output on a BST. The Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) of two nodes is the deepest node that has both as descendants, found recursively: if a node matches either target, or both targets are found in different subtrees, that node is the answer.

lessons.title: Graphs: Detecting a Cycle
lessons.content: In a directed graph, a cycle exists if DFS ever revisits a node that's currently on the active recursion path (not just previously visited overall). Tracking a separate 'in current path' set alongside the usual 'visited' set is what distinguishes 'already fully explored, no cycle' from 'currently being explored, cycle found'.

lessons.title: Dynamic Programming: Longest Common Subsequence
lessons.content: Find the longest sequence of characters that appears (in order, not necessarily contiguous) in both strings. A 2D table dp[i][j] holds the LCS length of the first i characters of one string and the first j of the other — if the characters match, extend the diagonal; otherwise take the best of skipping one character from either string. Use cases: text diffing, resource allocation, sequence alignment (also the basis for the Knapsack problem's table-building approach).
